blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Mesolithic Age serves as a transitional phase between the Paleolithic and Neolithic periods, coinciding with a warmer and drier climate.
Characterized by microliths—tiny, geometric stone tools (1–8 cm) hafted onto bone or wood handles to make arrows and spears.
Earliest evidence of animal domestication in India emerges during this period at Bagor (Rajasthan) and Adamgarh (Madhya Pradesh).
Human lifestyle shifted toward semi-permanent settlements, fishing, gathering, and hunting using improved projectile tools.
Rock art flourished, with Bhimbetka cave paintings extensively depicting hunting scenes, community dances, and social life.

blocks.content: The Mesolithic Age was a transitional phase from food gathering to food producing, marked by the widespread use of microliths and early animal domestication.

rows: Large, unpolished stone tools (choppers, hand axes)
Microliths (1–8 cm geometric tools hafted on wood/bone)
Nomadic hunting and wild plant gathering
Hunting, fishing, gathering, and early animal domestication
Fully nomadic life in caves and open grounds

items: Microliths (1–8 cm geometric stone tools) are exclusively associated with the Mesolithic Age in Indian history questions.
Bagor in Rajasthan is frequently tested as the largest Mesolithic site in India and a primary site for early animal domestication.
Bhimbetka rock shelters in Madhya Pradesh are a high-yield topic for questions on prehistoric art and Mesolithic social activities.
